issues.legal_issue: An administrative authority may disregard an earlier order that was not duly made because an interested party was denied the required opportunity to be heard, even though the authority has no general power of review.
material_facts: A consolidation petition was dismissed when the petitioner was absent.
The petitioner promptly sought restoration, supported by an affidavit explaining that illness had prevented attendance.
The Additional Director accepted that explanation and, after examining the records, acted under the authority’s statutory powers.
The Supreme Court treated the lack of an opportunity to be heard as preventing the earlier order from being a duly passed order.
issues.conclusion: The earlier order could be treated as invalid and disregarded; the absence of a general review power did not prevent the authority from acting in these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 42 of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948 makes notice to interested parties and an opportunity to be heard conditions precedent to varying an order, scheme, or repartition. Although Section 42 confers no general power of review, Harbhajan Singh v. Karan Singh does not govern an order that was not duly passed because the required hearing was unavailable; such an order may be ignored.

predicates.consolidation_revision_proceeding: An authority was considering a matter concerning the consolidation of holdings.
predicates.interested_party_denied_hearing: An interested party was not given an opportunity to be heard before the earlier order was made.
predicates.absence_caused_by_illness: The interested party’s absence that led to the earlier order was caused by illness.

issues.definition: When a consolidation matter involves an interested party who missed the hearing because of illness, an earlier order made without that party being heard may be treated as invalid and ignored.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court should not interfere under Article 136 where the High Court has examined the record and the challenged administrative decision caused no injustice warranting intervention.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a High Court judgment refusing relief against the Additional Director’s order.
The High Court had examined the records and concluded that the appellant’s asserted entitlement based on a report did not displace the effect of the revenue entries.
The High Court found that no injustice had been caused to the appellant.
The Supreme Court considered the case unsuitable for interference under Article 136.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was dismissed, with each side bearing its own costs.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 permits the Supreme Court to decline appellate interference where, on the facts and circumstances, the challenged decision presents no sufficient ground for intervention. The Court relied on the High Court’s examination of the record and its finding that no injustice had been caused.

predicates.article_136_appeal: The matter before the Supreme Court is an appeal invoking its discretionary appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.high_court_examined_record: The High Court examined the relevant record in reviewing the challenged decision.
predicates.no_injustice_found: The courts found that the challenged decision caused no injustice requiring appellate intervention.

issues.definition: In an appeal invoking discretionary appellate jurisdiction, where the High Court examined the record and no injustice requiring intervention was found, the Supreme Court declines to interfere.

issues.legal_issue: A judgment declining to decide whether a person acquired rights through long possession does not prevent that person from asserting any such rights in later proceedings to dispossess them.
material_facts: The appellant claimed that long possession might have given rise to rights.
The Supreme Court did not determine who was in possession, for how long, or in what capacity.
The Court stated that any rights acquired through possession could be asserted in proceedings before a competent authority to dispossess the appellant.
issues.conclusion: The judgment did not affect any rights the appellant might have acquired through possession, which could be asserted in later proceedings to dispossess them.
issues.legal_principle: Where the Court expressly refrains from deciding the fact, duration, and character of possession, its ruling does not determine any rights that may have arisen from that possession; those rights may be asserted before a competent authority in proceedings to dispossess the person claiming them.

predicates.proceeding_does_not_determine_possession: The court does not decide whether a person acquired rights through long possession.
predicates.later_proceeding_seeks_dispossession: A later proceeding before a competent authority seeks to dispossess the person claiming those rights.

issues.definition: If a proceeding leaves a claim to rights from long possession undecided, that claim remains open for assertion in a later proceeding seeking dispossession.
